title: Learning from Noise: Effective-Rank Collapse and Out-of-Distribution Rejection in Restricted Boltzmann Machines
abstract: Restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) represent data by shaping an energy landscape over visible and hidden configurations, but their discriminative use is fragile under out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs: samples outside the training distribution can be absorbed into one of the learned class basins rather than rejected. Here, we analyze this failure mode through the spectrum of the induced visible--visible interaction $J=WW^{T}$, where \(W\) is the visible--hidden weight matrix. Relative to a Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix reference, conventional training spreads spectral weight into many weak, bulk-compatible directions, increasing the effective rank of $J$. When auxiliary random binary images are assigned to a rejection label during training, the learned interaction undergoes effective-rank collapse: weak bulk-like modes are depleted, spectral weight concentrates into fewer dominant eigendirections, and the effective rank of $J$ approaches that of the empirical data covariance matrix. The resulting RBM rejects structured OOD image datasets while preserving MNIST classification accuracy, showing that random auxiliary exposure can reshape both the interaction spectrum and the free-energy landscape of an energy-based classifier.
summary: This paper analyzes how Restricted Boltzmann Machines fail when presented with Out-of-Distribution data. By augmenting the training set with random noise, the model undergoes an 'effective-rank collapse' in its learned weight structure. This spectral reorganization successfully forces the model to reject OOD inputs while maintaining high accuracy on known data.
main_problem: Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) used for classification are fragile under Out-of-Distribution (OOD) inputs, tending to absorb novel samples into learned class basins instead of rejecting them.
main_result: Training the RBM with auxiliary random binary images causes an 'effective-rank collapse' in the visible-visible interaction matrix J. This reorganization successfully enhances OOD rejection capability without degrading performance on in-distribution data.
method: The analysis uses spectral properties of the induced weight matrix $J=WW^T$, quantified by an entropy-based effective rank ($	ext{reff}$), and examines the free energy landscape to diagnose structural changes.
model_or_system: The model is a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) defined over visible and hidden configurations. The analysis focuses on the spectral properties of the induced interaction matrix $J = WW^T$, comparing training protocols using only in-distribution data (MNIST) versus augmented data including random binary images.
key_observables: Effective rank ($	ext{reff}$), eigenvalue spectrum of $J$, OOD rejection accuracy, and free energy landscape $F(v_x, v_y)$.
important_parameters: The ratio of spectral weight to the Marchenko–Pastur reference, number of Gibbs sampling steps ($k$), and hidden layer size ($N_h$).
main_assumptions: The failure mode is structural and related to the spectral properties of $J$; $	ext{reff}$ is used as a robust measure of effective dimensionality.
figures_summary: Figures compare eigenvalue spectra evolution (Fig. 2) showing rank growth vs. collapse, free energy landscapes (Fig. 6) showing OOD samples shifting toward rejection basins, and performance metrics across different training protocols (Figs. 1, 3).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the spectral properties of RBMs trained on in-distribution data versus augmented data. It first establishes the failure mode using spectral analysis ($	ext{reff}$), then uses free energy calculations to show landscape reorganization, and finally confirms robustness across varying training parameters like $k$ (CD steps).
why_interesting: The work provides a rigorous mathematical framework linking information geometry (spectral rank) to generalization performance in deep learning models, which has parallels with understanding effective dimensionality in complex quantum many-body systems.
